name: Dielectric function as a causal response function
summary: ε(ω) and the Drude/Lorentz models are the archetypal linear-response functions: causality makes χ analytic in the upper half-plane, giving the Kramers–Kronig relations between refraction and absorption; Im ε measures dissipation, and Kubo's formula gives the optical conductivity from equilibrium current correlations.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Landau–Devonshire theory of ferroelectrics
summary: Spontaneous polarization in a ferroelectric is a Landau order parameter: expanding the free energy in P gives Curie–Weiss divergence of ε above T_c, hysteresis as metastable branches, and first- versus second-order transitions from the sign of the quartic term; ferromagnetic M and χ follow the same theory.

name: Shannon capacity limits of optical fibre
summary: Shannon's channel capacity bounds data rates in fibre networks; because Kerr nonlinearity makes noise grow with launch power, achievable spectral efficiency peaks at an optimum power (the nonlinear Shannon limit), tying information entropy to fibre physics.
sources: Shannon (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication". *Bell Syst. Tech. J.* 27, 379. [doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x)

name: The three-level maser as a Carnot engine
summary: A three-level maser pumped by a hot reservoir and relaxed by a cold one is a heat engine: each emitted photon converts heat to work with efficiency ν_s/ν_p, which population inversion forces to stay below the Carnot efficiency (Scovil and Schulz-DuBois 1959), the founding example of quantum heat engines.
sources: Scovil & Schulz-DuBois (1959). "Three-Level Masers as Heat Engines". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 2, 262. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.2.262](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.2.262)

name: Optical refrigeration and the entropy of light
summary: Anti-Stokes fluorescence cooling of solids removes heat by emitting broadband, isotropic fluorescence that carries more entropy than the narrow, collimated pump; Landau's entropy of radiation keeps the second law intact and bounds the cooling efficiency.

sources: Epstein et al. (1995). "Observation of laser-induced fluorescent cooling of a solid". *Nature* 377, 500. [doi:10.1038/377500a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/377500a0)

name: Chemical potential of light: photon BEC versus lasing
summary: When photons thermalize by repeated absorption and re-emission in a dye-filled microcavity, their number is conserved and they acquire a chemical potential; above a critical number they Bose-condense into the lowest cavity mode, distinct from lasing, which needs inversion. Luminescent radiation from LEDs and solar cells likewise carries μ = qV (Würfel's generalized Planck law).
sources: Klaers et al. (2010). "Bose–Einstein condensation of photons in an optical microcavity". *Nature* 468, 545. [arXiv:1007.4088](https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.4088)

name: Random and multimode lasers as photonic spin glasses
summary: Mode amplitudes of multimode lasers evolve under an effective Hamiltonian of four-mode couplings; with random couplings (random lasers) this is a spherical p-spin glass at an effective temperature set by noise over pump squared, and replica-symmetry breaking has been reported in shot-to-shot spectral fluctuations. Passive mode-locking is the ordered phase of the same theory.
breaks: Effective equilibrium holds only in a slow-amplitude mean-field limit; real lasers are open and dissipative, and the measured RSB overlaps are indirect.
sources: Ghofraniha et al. (2015). "Experimental evidence of replica symmetry breaking in random lasers". *Nature Commun.* 6, 6058. [doi:10.1038/ncomms7058](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms7058)
Parisi (1979). "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 1754. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754)

name: Einstein A and B coefficients from detailed balance
summary: Requiring two-level atoms in equilibrium with Planck radiation to obey detailed balance with Boltzmann populations fixes g₁B₁₂ = g₂B₂₁ and A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³; stimulated emission, the source of laser gain, is forced by the Bose–Einstein statistics of photons.

name: Thermal-noise floor of ultrastable reference cavities
summary: Brownian motion of mirror coatings and substrates, computed with the FDT from mechanical loss angles (Levin's direct approach), sets the fundamental stability limit of Fabry–Pérot-stabilized lasers used in optical clocks and gravitational-wave detectors.
sources: Numata, Kemery & Camp (2004). "Thermal-Noise Limit in the Frequency Stabilization of Lasers with Rigid Cavities". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 93, 250602. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.250602](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.250602)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Schawlow–Townes linewidth as phase diffusion
summary: Spontaneous emission kicks the laser phase randomly; above threshold the amplitude is pinned but the phase performs Brownian motion, so the field correlation decays exponentially and the line is a Lorentzian of Schawlow–Townes width, the Langevin/Fokker–Planck laser theory of Lax and Haken.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Laser threshold as a second-order phase transition
summary: Near threshold the single-mode laser field obeys a Langevin equation with a Landau-type potential whose quadratic coefficient changes sign with pump: the field amplitude is an order parameter with mean-field exponent β = 1/2, spontaneous emission is the noise, and the free phase behaves like a Goldstone mode.
map: \dot E=(a-b|E|^2)E+\xi(t)\ \Rightarrow\ V(E)=-\frac a2|E|^2+\frac b4|E|^4,\qquad a\propto P_{\rm pump}-P_{\rm th}
breaks: The laser is a driven-dissipative steady state with no free energy or detailed balance; finite photon number rounds the transition, and the effective temperature is set by spontaneous emission rather than a heat bath.
sources: DeGiorgio & Scully (1970). "Analogy between the Laser Threshold Region and a Second-Order Phase Transition". *Phys. Rev. A* 2, 1170. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.2.1170](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.2.1170)

name: Thermal emission engineering: radiative cooling and TPV
summary: Kirchhoff's law (emissivity equals absorptivity, from detailed balance) lets nanophotonic structures engineer thermal emission: daytime radiative cooling dumps heat into cold space through the 8–13 µm atmospheric window, and selective emitters push thermophotovoltaic conversion toward the Carnot and detailed-balance limits.
map: P_{\rm cool}=P_{\rm rad}(T)-P_{\rm atm}(T_{\rm amb})-P_{\rm sun}-P_{\rm cond},\qquad \epsilon(\lambda,\theta)=\alpha(\lambda,\theta)
sources: Raman et al. (2014). "Passive radiative cooling below ambient air temperature under direct sunlight". *Nature* 515, 540. [doi:10.1038/nature13883](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13883)
Shockley & Queisser (1961). "Detailed Balance Limit of Efficiency of p-n Junction Solar Cells". *J. Appl. Phys.* 32, 510. [doi:10.1063/1.1736034](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1736034)

name: Anderson localization of light
summary: Anderson localization is a wave-interference effect, so it applies to light: John proposed strong photon localization near the band edges of disordered photonic crystals, and transverse localization has been imaged in disordered photonic lattices. Photons have no interactions or Fermi sea, so optics isolates the single-particle physics.
breaks: Absorption mimics localization in transmission measurements, and in 3D dielectrics near-field dipole coupling may prevent true Anderson localization of light.
sources: Anderson (1958). "Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 1492. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492)

John (1987). "Strong localization of photons in certain disordered dielectric superlattices". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 2486. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2486](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2486)

name: Fluctuational electrodynamics and near-field heat transfer
summary: Rytov's fluctuational electrodynamics treats thermal emission as Maxwell fields radiated by random currents whose spectrum is fixed by the FDT (∝ Im ε). Between bodies closer than the thermal wavelength, evanescent surface plasmon and phonon polaritons carry heat orders of magnitude beyond the Stefan–Boltzmann limit; the same correlators give Casimir–Lifshitz forces.
sources: Polder & Van Hove (1971). "Theory of Radiative Heat Transfer between Closely Spaced Bodies". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3303. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3303](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3303)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Coherent Ising machines from degenerate OPOs
summary: A degenerate optical parametric oscillator above threshold settles into one of two phases (0 or π), an optical Ising spin; networks of time-multiplexed OPO pulses with measurement-feedback coupling search for low-energy states of Ising and Sherrington–Kirkpatrick Hamiltonians, using the pitchfork bifurcation as an annealing schedule.
sources: McMahon et al. (2016). "A fully programmable 100-spin coherent Ising machine with all-to-all connections". *Science* 354, 614. [doi:10.1126/science.aah5178](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aah5178)
Sherrington & Kirkpatrick (1975). "Solvable Model of a Spin-Glass". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 35, 1792. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792)

name: Optical thermodynamics of multimode nonlinear fibres
summary: In highly multimode nonlinear waveguides the conserved optical power and Hamiltonian play the roles of particle number and energy; weak Kerr mixing drives modal occupations to a Rayleigh–Jeans distribution with an optical temperature and chemical potential, and beam self-cleaning appears as condensation into the fundamental mode.
sources: Wu, Hassan & Christodoulides (2019). "Thermodynamic theory of highly multimoded nonlinear optical systems". *Nature Photon.* 13, 776. [doi:10.1038/s41566-019-0501-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41566-019-0501-7)

name: Optical NLS, inverse scattering and the Bethe ansatz
summary: Pulse propagation in a Kerr fibre obeys the integrable nonlinear Schrödinger equation, solved exactly by inverse scattering; its quantized form is the attractive delta-interacting Bose gas (Lieb–Liniger/McGuire), which Lai and Haus solved by Bethe ansatz to describe quantum optical solitons.
sources: Lai & Haus (1989). "Quantum theory of solitons in optical fibers. II. Exact solution". *Phys. Rev. A* 40, 854. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.40.854](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.40.854)

Lieb & Liniger (1963). "Exact Analysis of an Interacting Bose Gas. I. The General Solution and the Ground State". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 1605. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605)

name: Planck's resonators: dipole emission balances absorption
summary: Planck obtained the factor 8πν²/c³ classically by balancing the Larmor emission of damped Hertzian dipole oscillators against their absorption of isotropic radiation; quantizing the oscillator energy then gave the Planck spectrum, so antenna theory sits at the birth of quantum statistics.
sources: Planck (1901). "Ueber das Gesetz der Energieverteilung im Normalspectrum". *Ann. Phys.* 309, 553. [doi:10.1002/andp.19013090310](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19013090310)

name: Compton thermalization and the Kompaneets equation
summary: Repeated Compton scattering off a thermal electron gas drives photons toward a Bose–Einstein distribution with a chemical potential, since scattering conserves photon number. The Kompaneets Fokker–Planck equation, including the induced-scattering n² term, governs CMB μ- and y-distortions and the Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect.
map: \frac{\partial n}{\partial y}=\frac{1}{x^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[x^4\left(\frac{\partial n}{\partial x}+n+n^2\right)\right],\quad x=\frac{h\nu}{k_BT_e}
sources: Rybicki & Lightman (1979). "Radiative processes in astrophysics". Wiley. [doi:10.1002/9783527618170](https://doi.org/10.1002/9783527618170)
Mather et al. (1994). "Measurement of the cosmic microwave background spectrum by the COBE FIRAS instrument". *Astrophys. J.* 420, 439. [doi:10.1086/173574](https://doi.org/10.1086/173574)

name: Radiative transfer as a Boltzmann equation for photons
summary: The radiative-transfer equation is a linear Boltzmann equation for the photon distribution, with extinction as the loss term and the scattering phase function as the collision kernel; its diffusion limit gives the Rosseland opacity of stellar interiors and diffuse optics in tissue, just as Chapman–Enskog gives transport coefficients.

sources: Rybicki & Lightman (1979). "Radiative processes in astrophysics". Wiley. [doi:10.1002/9783527618170](https://doi.org/10.1002/9783527618170)

name: Rayleigh–Brillouin spectrum and the dynamic structure factor
summary: Light inelastically scattered by a fluid shows a central Rayleigh line (heat diffusion) and two Brillouin lines (sound); their widths and the Landau–Placzek intensity ratio come from the hydrodynamic dynamic structure factor S(q,ω), which by the FDT is the absorptive part of the density response.

name: Dynamic light scattering measures Brownian motion
summary: Light scattered by diffusing particles decorrelates as g⁽¹⁾(q,τ) = exp(−Dq²τ); with the Siegert relation and Stokes–Einstein D = k_BT/6πηa, photon-correlation spectroscopy turns Einstein's Brownian-motion theory into a routine size and dynamics probe, extended to multiple scattering by diffusing-wave spectroscopy.
sources: Einstein (1905). "Über die von der molekularkinetischen Theorie der Wärme geforderte Bewegung von in ruhenden Flüssigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen". *Ann. Phys.* 322, 549. [doi:10.1002/andp.19053220806](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053220806)
Pusey & van Megen (1986). "Phase behaviour of concentrated suspensions of nearly hard colloidal spheres". *Nature* 320, 340. [doi:10.1038/320340a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/320340a0)

name: Optical traps as the laboratory for fluctuation theorems
summary: The gradient force on a Rayleigh-regime dielectric particle, F = ½ Re(α)∇|E|², makes a tunable harmonic or double-well potential for a Brownian colloid; optical traps gave the first tests of fluctuation theorems and the measurement of Landauer's k_BT ln 2 erasure bound.
map: \mathbf F_{\rm grad}=\tfrac12\mathrm{Re}(\alpha)\nabla\langle|\mathbf E|^2\rangle,\qquad \kappa\langle x^2\rangle=k_BT,\qquad \langle W_{\rm erase}\rangle\ge k_BT\ln2
sources: Ashkin (1970). "Acceleration and Trapping of Particles by Radiation Pressure". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 24, 156. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156)
Bérut et al. (2012). "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics". *Nature* 483, 187. [doi:10.1038/nature10872](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872)

name: Critical opalescence and Ornstein–Zernike scattering
summary: Rayleigh scattering from a fluid measures its density fluctuations, I ∝ S(q) with S(0) = nk_BTκ_T (Einstein–Smoluchowski). Near a critical point κ_T and ξ diverge and the fluid turns milky; the Ornstein–Zernike angular dependence of the scattered light was a primary measurement of γ, ν and η.
sources: Einstein (1910). "Theorie der Opaleszenz von homogenen Flüssigkeiten und Flüssigkeitsgemischen in der Nähe des kritischen Zustandes". *Ann. Phys.* 338, 1275. [doi:10.1002/andp.19103381612](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19103381612)

name: Thermodynamics derived from statistical mechanics
summary: Every classical-thermodynamic potential is the logarithm of a partition function, and the laws become theorems about counting states. Thermodynamics is the macroscopic shadow of the ensemble.
map: U=-\partial_\beta\ln Z,\ F=-k_BT\ln Z,\ S=k_B\ln W

name: Onsager theory and efficiency at maximum power
summary: In the Onsager linear-response regime a tightly coupled engine at maximum power has η=η_C/2, the first-order term of Curzon–Ahlborn. The thermoelectric figure of merit ZT is a ratio of Onsager coefficients.
sources: Van den Broeck (2005). "Thermodynamic Efficiency at Maximum Power". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 95, 190602. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.190602](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.190602)
Onsager (1931). "Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.". *Phys. Rev.* 37, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.37.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.37.405)

name: Stochastic and microscopic heat engines
summary: Stochastic thermodynamics defines heat and work for a single colloid in a modulated optical trap, which has been run as a micrometre-scale Stirling engine. Thermodynamic uncertainty relations add a bound: power, efficiency and power fluctuations cannot all be optimal.
sources: Blickle & Bechinger (2012). "Realization of a micrometre-sized stochastic heat engine". *Nat. Phys.* 8, 143. [doi:10.1038/nphys2163](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys2163)

Pietzonka & Seifert (2018). "Universal Trade-Off between Power, Efficiency, and Constancy in Steady-State Heat Engines". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 120, 190602. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.120.190602](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.120.190602)

name: Critical working media for heat engines
summary: An engine whose working substance sits near a critical point can approach Carnot efficiency at finite power. The diverging heat capacity can outweigh critical slowing down in suitable universality classes, and Ising-model engines test the idea.
sources: Campisi & Fazio (2016). "The power of a critical heat engine". *Nat. Commun.* 7, 11895. [doi:10.1038/ncomms11895](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms11895)

name: Maxwell's demon, Gibbs paradox and the second law
summary: Entropy read as missing information resolves both the Gibbs mixing paradox (distinguishability is information) and Maxwell's demon (erasing the demon's memory costs k_BT ln 2 per bit). The Kelvin–Planck statement survives once information is booked as a thermodynamic resource.
sources: Landauer (1961). "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process". *IBM J. Res. Dev.* 5, 183. [doi:10.1147/rd.53.0183](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183)
Bérut et al. (2012). "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics". *Nature* 483, 187. [doi:10.1038/nature10872](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872)

name: Third law from quantum ground states
summary: Nernst's theorem follows from quantum statistics: a non-degenerate ground state gives S→0, and degenerate gases have C∝T (fermions) or T^{3/2} (bosons) and phonons C∝T³. The classical ideal gas, with S∝ln T, violates the third law.

name: H-theorem: a dynamical second law
summary: Boltzmann's H-function is minus the entropy, and the Stosszahlansatz makes dH/dt≤0. Loschmidt's reversibility paradox and Zermelo's recurrence paradox show that the arrow of time comes from the low-entropy initial condition and from coarse-graining.

name: Second law as the average of fluctuation theorems
summary: The Clausius inequality is the mean of an exact trajectory identity: the integral fluctuation theorem gives <Δs_tot> ≥ 0 by Jensen's inequality, and Jarzynski gives <W> ≥ ΔF. Single trajectories can violate the second law, but only with exponentially small probability.
map: \langle e^{-\Delta s_{tot}/k_B}\rangle=1\Rightarrow\langle\Delta s_{tot}\rangle\ge0;\ \langle e^{-\beta W}\rangle=e^{-\beta\Delta F}\Rightarrow\langle W\rangle\ge\Delta F
sources: Jarzynski (1997). "Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 78, 2690. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690)
Seifert (2012). "Stochastic thermodynamics, fluctuation theorems and molecular machines". *Rep. Prog. Phys.* 75, 126001. [arXiv:1205.4176](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.4176)

name: Bose condensation obeys Clausius–Clapeyron
summary: In the p–T plane the ideal Bose gas behaves like a first-order condensation in momentum space. Its transition line p_c∝T^{5/2} obeys Clausius–Clapeyron with a latent heat of (5/2)k_BT ζ(5/2)/ζ(3/2) per particle.

name: Nucleation as thermally activated barrier crossing
summary: A metastable phase decays across a first-order transition by Kramers escape over the free-energy barrier of the critical nucleus. Surface tension and the difference in chemical potential between the phases set the height of that barrier.
sources: Kramers (1940). "Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion model of chemical reactions". *Physica* 7, 284. [doi:10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2)

name: Liquid–gas critical point in the 3D Ising class
summary: The end point of the liquid–vapour line, where the Clausius–Clapeyron latent heat vanishes, has 3D Ising exponents (β≈0.326, γ≈1.237). Critical opalescence is the visible sign of the diverging compressibility.

name: Lattice-gas isomorphism: fluids and magnets
summary: The substitution n_i=(1+s_i)/2 maps a lattice gas exactly onto the Ising model, with chemical potential corresponding to field and coexistence to h=0. This is why liquid–gas, binary-alloy and uniaxial-magnet critical points share exponents.
sources: Lee & Yang (1952). "Statistical Theory of Equations of State and Phase Transitions. II. Lattice Gas and Ising Model". *Phys. Rev.* 87, 410. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.87.410](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.87.410)

name: Van der Waals and Maxwell construction as mean field
summary: The van der Waals equation is the mean-field (Landau) theory of the liquid–gas transition. The Maxwell equal-area construction resolves its loop, and it predicts the mean-field exponents β=1/2 and δ=3.
breaks: Real fluids have 3D Ising exponents (β≈0.326), not mean-field ones; van der Waals neglects the fluctuations that dominate below d=4.

name: Potentials as logarithms of partition functions
summary: Each Legendre-transformed potential belongs to an ensemble: S to the microcanonical, F to the canonical, Ω to the grand canonical and G to the isothermal–isobaric. Response functions such as C_V and κ_T are variances in the matching ensemble.

name: Onsager reciprocity as dynamical Maxwell relations
summary: Maxwell relations follow from the symmetry of second derivatives of a state function, and Onsager's L_ij=L_ji follows from microscopic reversibility. Both yield cross-effect equalities, such as the Kelvin relation Π=TS between the Peltier and Seebeck coefficients.
map: (\partial S/\partial V)_T=(\partial p/\partial T)_V\ \leftrightarrow\ J_i=\sum_jL_{ij}X_j,\ L_{ij}=L_{ji}
breaks: Maxwell relations are exact equilibrium identities of a state function. Onsager symmetry needs time-reversal invariance (L_ij(B)=L_ji(-B)), holds only in linear response, and has no generating potential beyond the dissipation function.
sources: Onsager (1931). "Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.". *Phys. Rev.* 37, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.37.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.37.405)

name: Landau functions and the convexity of potentials
summary: A coarse-grained Landau free energy can be non-convex, but the true thermodynamic potential is its convex envelope (Legendre–Fenchel). The stability conditions C_V>0 and κ_T>0 select the Maxwell construction, and spinodals mark where they fail locally.

name: Harris criterion: when disorder changes universality
summary: Weak quenched bond disorder is relevant at a clean critical point when dν<2, equivalently α>0. The system then flows to a random fixed point with new exponents, so whether disorder matters is decided by the clean universality class.
sources: Harris (1974). "Effect of random defects on the critical behaviour of Ising models". *J. Phys. C* 7, 1671. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/7/9/009](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/7/9/009)

name: Epidemic thresholds as absorbing-state transitions
summary: SIS and contact-process epidemics are absorbing-state transitions of a non-equilibrium steady state, in the directed-percolation class on lattices. On scale-free networks the heterogeneous mean-field threshold vanishes for γ≤3.
sources: Pastor-Satorras & Vespignani (2001). "Epidemic Spreading in Scale-Free Networks". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 86, 3200. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.86.3200](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.86.3200)
Hinrichsen (2000). "Non-equilibrium critical phenomena and phase transitions into absorbing states". *Adv. Phys.* 49, 815. [arXiv:cond-mat/0001070](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0001070)

name: Critical phenomena on scale-free networks
summary: Ising, percolation and epidemic transitions on networks are controlled by moments of the degree distribution. For P(k)~k^{-γ} the exponents depend on γ, and for γ≤3 the Ising T_c diverges and the percolation threshold vanishes because <k²> diverges.
map: T_c^{\text{Ising}}\propto\langle k^2\rangle/\langle k\rangle;\ p_c=\frac{\langle k\rangle}{\langle k^2\rangle-\langle k\rangle}
sources: Dorogovtsev, Goltsev & Mendes (2008). "Critical phenomena in complex networks". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 80, 1275. [arXiv:0705.0010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.0010)

name: MBL l-bits as emergent integrability
summary: Fully many-body-localized systems have an extensive set of quasi-local conserved l-bits, an emergent counterpart of the integrals of motion of Bethe-ansatz models. Both evade ordinary thermalization: integrable systems relax to a generalized Gibbs ensemble, and MBL systems retain memory of local initial conditions.
breaks: Bethe-ansatz integrability is fine-tuned and destroyed by generic perturbations, whereas l-bits are quasi-local and claimed to be robust. Whether MBL survives the thermodynamic limit is disputed (Sierant et al. 2024).
sources: Nandkishore & Huse (2015). "Many-Body Localization and Thermalization in Quantum Statistical Mechanics". *Annu. Rev. Condens. Matter Phys.* 6, 15. [arXiv:1404.0686](https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.0686)

Basko, Aleiner & Altshuler (2006). "Metal–insulator transition in a weakly interacting many-electron system with localized single-particle states". *Ann. Phys.* 321, 1126. [arXiv:cond-mat/0506617](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0506617)

name: Weak localization as a failure of Boltzmann transport
summary: Boltzmann (Drude) transport adds scattering probabilities and so ignores interference. Coherent backscattering along time-reversed paths gives the weak-localization correction, logarithmic in 2D, and the Boltzmann description fails completely at the Ioffe–Regel limit k_F l ~ 1.
sources: Abrahams et al. (1979). "Scaling Theory of Localization: Absence of Quantum Diffusion in Two Dimensions". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 42, 673. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.673](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.673)

name: One-parameter scaling theory of localization
summary: The 'gang of four' recast Anderson localization as an RG flow of the dimensionless conductance g with system size. Because β(g)<0 for all g in d≤2, there is no metal there. In d=3 an unstable fixed point g_c is the mobility edge, a critical point with ν≈1.57 (orthogonal class).
sources: Abrahams et al. (1979). "Scaling Theory of Localization: Absence of Quantum Diffusion in Two Dimensions". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 42, 673. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.673](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.673)
Anderson (1958). "Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 1492. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492)

name: Directed percolation and absorbing states
summary: Absorbing-state transitions in driven systems (the contact process, epidemics, catalysis) generically belong to the directed-percolation class, which is percolation with a preferred time direction.
sources: Hinrichsen (2000). "Non-equilibrium critical phenomena and phase transitions into absorbing states". *Adv. Phys.* 49, 815. [arXiv:cond-mat/0001070](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0001070)

name: Percolation as a universality class
summary: Percolation is a geometric critical point with its own exponents, which obey the same scaling and hyperscaling relations as thermal transitions. In 2D they are known exactly from Coulomb-gas and SLE methods.

name: Fortuin–Kasteleyn: percolation is the q→1 Potts model
summary: The random-cluster representation writes the q-state Potts partition function as a sum over bond clusters weighted by q^{N_c}. Taking q→1 gives bond percolation and q=2 gives Ising, whose spin correlations equal FK-cluster connectivities. This is also the basis of Swendsen–Wang cluster Monte Carlo.
sources: Fortuin & Kasteleyn (1972). "On the random-cluster model: I. Introduction and relation to other models". *Physica* 57, 536. [doi:10.1016/0031-8914(72)90045-6](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-8914(72)90045-6)
Swendsen & Wang (1987). "Nonuniversal critical dynamics in Monte Carlo simulations". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 86. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86)

name: Real-space RG for percolation
summary: Kadanoff's block-spin idea applied to percolation renormalizes the occupation probability cell by cell, p'=R_b(p). The nontrivial fixed point approximates p_c, and ν follows from the linearized flow. Percolation is the cleanest teaching case of position-space RG.

name: Aging and FDT violation in glassy dynamics
summary: Spin glasses out of equilibrium age, and their two-time response and correlation violate the FDT in a quasi-universal way that defines an effective temperature T/X. The dynamical solution of mean-field models ties X to the Parisi order-parameter function.
sources: Cugliandolo & Kurchan (1993). "Analytical solution of the off-equilibrium dynamics of a long-range spin-glass model". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 71, 173. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.173](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.173)

name: Edwards–Anderson: Ising with quenched random bonds
summary: The Edwards–Anderson spin glass is the Ising Hamiltonian with random-sign couplings. Frustrated plaquettes, not disorder by itself, destroy ferromagnetic order (a Mattis gauge transform removes unfrustrated disorder), and the order parameter becomes q_EA.
map: H=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}s_is_j,\ J_{ij}=\pm J;\ q_{EA}=\overline{\langle s_i\rangle^2}
sources: Edwards & Anderson (1975). "Theory of spin glasses". *J. Phys. F* 5, 965. [doi:10.1088/0305-4608/5/5/017](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4608/5/5/017)

name: SK model: exact mean field for spin glasses
summary: The infinite-range SK model is the spin-glass analogue of Curie–Weiss. Mean field is exact there, but it needs replicas and Parisi's replica-symmetry breaking. TAP equations give the self-consistent local magnetizations, including the Onsager reaction term.
sources: Sherrington & Kirkpatrick (1975). "Solvable Model of a Spin-Glass". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 35, 1792. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792)
Thouless, Anderson & Palmer (1977). "Solution of 'Solvable model of a spin glass'". *Phil. Mag.* 35, 593. [doi:10.1080/14786437708235992](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786437708235992)
Parisi (1979). "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 1754. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754)

name: Droplet scaling vs RSB in finite dimensions
summary: Fisher–Huse droplet theory describes short-range spin glasses by zero-temperature RG scaling, with a stiffness exponent θ and a single pair of pure states. It is the main rival to the mean-field RSB picture, and which is right in d=3 is unsettled.
sources: Fisher & Huse (1986). "Ordered Phase of Short-Range Ising Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 56, 1601. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.1601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.1601)

name: Maximum-entropy models of neural data
summary: Maximizing entropy subject to measured means and pairwise correlations gives exactly a pairwise Ising (Boltzmann-machine) distribution. Fitted to retinal spike trains, it showed that weak pairwise correlations imply strongly collective states. Boltzmann-machine learning minimizes the KL divergence to the data.
map: \max S[p]\ \text{s.t.}\ \langle s_i\rangle,\langle s_is_j\rangle\Rightarrow p\propto e^{\sum h_is_i+\sum J_{ij}s_is_j}
sources: Jaynes (1957). "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev.* 106, 620. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.106.620](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.106.620)
Schneidman et al. (2006). "Weak pairwise correlations imply strongly correlated network states in a neural population". *Nature* 440, 1007. [arXiv:q-bio/0512013](https://arxiv.org/abs/q-bio/0512013)

name: Diffusion models reverse a Fokker–Planck process
summary: Score-based diffusion models add noise to data with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (Langevin) SDE, then generate samples by integrating the time-reversed SDE, whose drift contains the learned score ∇ln p_t. Stochastic gradient descent is itself often modelled as Langevin dynamics at an effective temperature.
sources: Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015). "Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics". *ICML*. [arXiv:1503.03585](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03585)
Song et al. (2021). "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations". *ICLR*. [arXiv:2011.13456](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456)

name: Boltzmann machines are inverse Ising models
summary: Hopfield networks and Boltzmann machines are Ising or spin-glass Hamiltonians with learned couplings. Learning fits J_ij and h_i until model correlations match data (the inverse Ising problem), and sampling uses Glauber or Metropolis dynamics.
map: P(s)\propto e^{-E(s)},\ E=-\tfrac12\sum w_{ij}s_is_j-\sum b_is_i;\ \Delta w_{ij}\propto\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\text{data}}-\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\text{model}}
sources: Hopfield (1982). "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities". *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.* 79, 2554. [doi:10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554)
Ackley, Hinton & Sejnowski (1985). "A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines". *Cognitive Science* 9, 147. [doi:10.1207/s15516709cog0901_7](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog0901_7)

name: Mean-field limits of neural networks
summary: At infinite width, training a two-layer network becomes a nonlinear PDE for the density of neurons in parameter space: a mean-field theory exact at large N, like Curie–Weiss. Approximate message passing is the TAP equations applied to inference problems.
sources: Mei, Montanari & Nguyen (2018). "A mean field view of the landscape of two-layer neural networks". *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.* 115, E7665. [arXiv:1804.06561](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.06561)

name: Renormalization group and deep learning
summary: Coarse-graining layer by layer in deep networks resembles block-spin RG. One variational-RG scheme maps exactly onto stacked restricted Boltzmann machines, and networks trained on 2D Ising samples learn block-spin-like features.
breaks: RG by design keeps only long-wavelength information. Generic learning keeps whatever predicts the target and need not have a fixed point or a scale hierarchy, and the exact mapping holds for one variational scheme only.
sources: Mehta & Schwab (2014). "An exact mapping between the Variational Renormalization Group and Deep Learning". [arXiv:1410.3831](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3831)

name: Mermin–Wagner and the limits of 2D order
summary: The Mermin–Wagner theorem, a statement about thermal fluctuations of Goldstone modes in equilibrium ensembles, forbids continuous-symmetry long-range order at T>0 in d≤2. That leaves room for BKT quasi-long-range order and makes a 2D ideal Bose gas uncondensable.
sources: Mermin & Wagner (1966). "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 17, 1133. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133)

name: Maxwell–Boltzmann as the Boltzmann-equation fixed point
summary: The stationary solution of the Boltzmann collision integral is the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, the one-particle marginal of the canonical ensemble. Kinetic theory thus derives ensemble equilibrium dynamically, given molecular chaos.
map: C[f]=0\Leftrightarrow f\propto e^{-\beta m(\mathbf v-\mathbf u)^2/2}

name: Static fluctuation–response identities
summary: The static limit of the fluctuation–dissipation theorem equates susceptibilities with ensemble variances. C_V, χ and κ_T measure the fluctuations of energy, magnetization and particle number, so a diverging response at criticality is the same thing as diverging fluctuations.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Fokker–Planck stationary state is the Boltzmann distribution
summary: With detailed balance and the Einstein relation D=k_BT/γ, the Smoluchowski equation relaxes to P∝e^{-βU}. Langevin thermostats and Metropolis Monte Carlo are built to sample the canonical ensemble this way.

name: Jarzynski free energies as partition-function ratios
summary: Jarzynski's equality computes the equilibrium ratio Z_B/Z_A from non-equilibrium work samples. It is used to extract free energies from single-molecule pulling and from fast-switching simulations, alongside thermodynamic integration.
sources: Jarzynski (1997). "Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 78, 2690. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690)

Crooks (1999). "Entropy production fluctuation theorem and the nonequilibrium work relation for free energy differences". *Phys. Rev. E* 60, 2721. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.60.2721](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.60.2721)

name: Mean field as a variational bound on Z
summary: Weiss and Bragg–Williams mean-field theory is the optimal product-state trial in the Gibbs–Bogoliubov–Feynman inequality. That makes it a controlled variational approximation to ln Z, exact when each spin has infinitely many neighbours.

name: Information engines and feedback fluctuation theorems
summary: Measurement and feedback (Maxwell's demon, the Szilard engine) enter the second law through the mutual information. The Sagawa–Ueda equality generalizes Jarzynski, and Landauer erasure closes the cycle. Both have been tested in colloidal and single-electron experiments.
sources: Sagawa & Ueda (2010). "Generalized Jarzynski Equality under Nonequilibrium Feedback Control". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 104, 090602. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.090602](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.090602)
Parrondo, Horowitz & Sagawa (2015). "Thermodynamics of information". *Nat. Phys.* 11, 131. [doi:10.1038/nphys3230](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys3230)
Bérut et al. (2012). "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics". *Nature* 483, 187. [doi:10.1038/nature10872](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872)

name: TASEP and KPZ: exactly solvable non-equilibrium models
summary: TASEP is solved exactly by the Bethe ansatz and by a matrix-product ansatz, which give its boundary-driven phase diagram. Its height function is a discrete KPZ interface whose fluctuations follow the Tracy–Widom laws of random matrices.
sources: Derrida et al. (1993). "Exact solution of a 1D asymmetric exclusion model using a matrix formulation". *J. Phys. A* 26, 1493. [doi:10.1088/0305-4470/26/7/011](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/26/7/011)
Johansson (1999). "Shape Fluctuations and Random Matrices". *Commun. Math. Phys.* 209, 437. [arXiv:math/9903134](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9903134)

name: Exact solutions as benchmarks for phase transitions
summary: Onsager's solution of the 2D Ising model was the first proof that a partition function can become non-analytic, which settled whether statistical mechanics can describe phase transitions at all. Vertex and Bethe-ansatz models supply further exact critical points.
sources: Onsager (1944). "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition". *Phys. Rev.* 65, 117. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.65.117](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)

name: Exact exponents anchor universality classes
summary: Exactly solved models fix the exponents of whole classes, for example 2D Ising (α=0 log, β=1/8, γ=7/4, ν=1). Baxter's eight-vertex model has continuously varying exponents, which shows that naive universality can fail along marginal lines.
sources: Onsager (1944). "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition". *Phys. Rev.* 65, 117. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.65.117](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)

name: Onsager transfer-matrix solution of 2D Ising
summary: The transfer-matrix method in the solvable-models note is how the 2D Ising model was solved. Z=Tr T^N reduces to the largest eigenvalue, which gives T_c, the logarithmic specific heat and β=1/8.
sources: Onsager (1944). "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition". *Phys. Rev.* 65, 117. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.65.117](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)

name: Six-vertex F-model and KT-type transitions
summary: The six-vertex F-model, the XXZ chain and the Lieb–Liniger gas are exactly solvable realizations of Kosterlitz–Thouless physics. Through the BCSOS mapping the F-model transition is an infinite-order roughening transition, and the gapless phases are Luttinger liquids with quasi-long-range order.
sources: van Beijeren (1977). "Exactly solvable model for the roughening transition of a crystal surface". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 38, 993. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.38.993](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.38.993)

Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)

name: Quantum Boltzmann equation and BE/FD equilibria
summary: With Pauli-blocking and Bose-enhancement factors (1±f) in the collision integral (Uehling–Uhlenbeck, Nordheim), the stationary state becomes the Bose–Einstein or Fermi–Dirac distribution. This is the basis of electron and phonon Boltzmann transport.
map: C[f]\propto\int[f_3f_4(1\pm f_1)(1\pm f_2)-f_1f_2(1\pm f_3)(1\pm f_4)]\Rightarrow f=(e^{\beta(\epsilon-\mu)}\mp1)^{-1}

name: The lambda transition and the 3D XY class
summary: Interacting Bose condensation, as in helium-4, is a continuous transition in the 3D XY (O(2)) class. The space-shuttle value α≈-0.0127 is the most precisely measured critical exponent. The ideal Bose gas falls instead in the spherical-model class.
sources: Lipa et al. (2003). "Specific heat of liquid helium in zero gravity very near the lambda point". *Phys. Rev. B* 68, 174518. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.68.174518](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.68.174518)

name: 2D Bose gas: no BEC but a BKT superfluid
summary: An ideal 2D Bose gas has no condensate at T>0, because the Bose–Einstein integral diverges. With interactions it becomes superfluid by vortex unbinding at the BKT transition, at phase-space density nλ²≈ln(ξ/g̃), as observed in trapped atomic gases.
sources: Hadzibabic et al. (2006). "Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless crossover in a trapped atomic gas". *Nature* 441, 1118. [arXiv:cond-mat/0605291](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0605291)

Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)

name: Non-equilibrium universality classes
summary: Directed percolation, KPZ and conserved-sandpile classes extend universality to steady states without detailed balance. They carry independent dynamic exponents and lack the fluctuation–dissipation constraints of equilibrium classes.
sources: Hinrichsen (2000). "Non-equilibrium critical phenomena and phase transitions into absorbing states". *Adv. Phys.* 49, 815. [arXiv:cond-mat/0001070](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0001070)

name: Dynamic RG for KPZ and driven interfaces
summary: Wilson's RG extended to stochastic PDEs (dynamic RG) gives the KPZ exponents. Galilean invariance fixes χ+z=2, and in 1+1D z=3/2 and χ=1/2 exactly, the standard example of RG for non-equilibrium universality.
sources: Kardar, Parisi & Zhang (1986). "Dynamic Scaling of Growing Interfaces". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 56, 889. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889)

name: Dynamic critical phenomena and critical slowing down
summary: Near T_c the relaxation time diverges as τ~ξ^z. The Hohenberg–Halperin dynamic classes (models A–J) depend on conservation laws and mode couplings as well as static symmetry, and the dynamic susceptibility probes them through the FDT.
sources: Hohenberg & Halperin (1977). "Theory of dynamic critical phenomena". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 49, 435. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.49.435](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.49.435)

name: Thermodynamics extended to quantum systems
summary: Quantum thermodynamics keeps the laws (energy balance, Clausius inequality, Carnot bound) but defines work and heat for density matrices and open-system maps. Coherence and entanglement act as additional resources or costs.
map: dU=\mathrm{Tr}(\dot\rho H)+\mathrm{Tr}(\rho\dot H)=\dot Q+\dot W;\ \Delta S\ge\beta Q

name: Quantum heat engines and refrigerators
summary: Otto, Carnot and absorption cycles run with qubits, oscillators and spins as working media; the Carnot bound survives with thermal baths. Non-thermal (squeezed, coherent) reservoirs can exceed η_C because they are not heat in the classical sense.

name: Third law and second laws in the quantum regime
summary: The unattainability principle has been derived and quantified for quantum systems: cooling time diverges as T→0, with a bound set by the bath's density of states. For small systems the second law splits into a family of single-shot conditions.
sources: Masanes & Oppenheim (2017). "A general derivation and quantification of the third law of thermodynamics". *Nat. Commun.* 8, 14538. [arXiv:1412.3828](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.3828)

name: Anderson localization and MBL in cold atoms
summary: Optical speckle and quasiperiodic lattices made matter-wave Anderson localization directly visible (exponential density profiles), and interacting fermions in quasiperiodic lattices kept memory of an initial density wave, the first MBL signature.
sources: Billy et al. (2008). "Direct observation of Anderson localization of matter waves in a controlled disorder". *Nature* 453, 891. [arXiv:0804.1621](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.1621)
Schreiber et al. (2015). "Observation of many-body localization of interacting fermions in a quasirandom optical lattice". *Science* 349, 842. [arXiv:1501.05661](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.05661)

name: MBL-protected discrete time crystals
summary: Generic periodically driven many-body systems heat to infinite temperature. MBL prevents this and allows period-doubled spatiotemporal order, the discrete time crystal, which is stable to perturbations of the drive.
sources: Else, Bauer & Nayak (2016). "Floquet Time Crystals". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 117, 090402. [arXiv:1603.08001](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.08001)

name: Hatano–Nelson: non-Hermitian localization from flux lines
summary: Non-Hermitian quantum mechanics as a field grew from the statistical mechanics of flux lines pinned by columnar defects in superconductors. An imaginary vector potential (tilted field) delocalizes Anderson states, the first non-Hermitian localization transition and the ancestor of the non-Hermitian skin effect.
sources: Hatano & Nelson (1996). "Localization Transitions in Non-Hermitian Quantum Mechanics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 77, 570. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.570](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.570)

name: Level statistics: Poisson vs Wigner–Dyson
summary: Spectral statistics diagnose both Anderson/MB localization and quantum chaos: localized states give Poisson level spacings, and ergodic or extended states give random-matrix (GOE) repulsion. The ratio ⟨r⟩ is the standard order parameter for the MBL transition.
sources: Oganesyan & Huse (2007). "Localization of interacting fermions at high temperature". *Phys. Rev. B* 75, 155111. [arXiv:cond-mat/0610854](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0610854)

name: Many-body localization as ETH failure
summary: MBL is the main known mechanism by which an interacting, non-integrable quantum system violates ETH. Eigenstates have area-law entanglement and Poisson level statistics, and local memory survives forever.
sources: Nandkishore & Huse (2015). "Many-Body Localization and Thermalization in Quantum Statistical Mechanics". *Annu. Rev. Condens. Matter Phys.* 6, 15. [arXiv:1404.0686](https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.0686)

Basko, Aleiner & Altshuler (2006). "Metal–insulator transition in a weakly interacting many-electron system with localized single-particle states". *Ann. Phys.* 321, 1126. [arXiv:cond-mat/0506617](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0506617)

name: Measurement-induced transitions and percolation
summary: In monitored random circuits, the zeroth Rényi entanglement entropy maps exactly onto a minimal cut through a percolation cluster. The measurement-induced volume-to-area-law transition therefore becomes classical percolation in this limit, and higher Rényi entropies flow to distinct non-percolation classes.
sources: Skinner, Ruhman & Nahum (2019). "Measurement-Induced Phase Transitions in the Dynamics of Entanglement". *Phys. Rev. X* 9, 031009. [arXiv:1808.05953](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05953)

name: Percolation thresholds for photonic cluster states
summary: Probabilistic fusion gates build random lattices of entangled photons, and a cluster state usable for universal measurement-based computation exists only above the bond-percolation threshold. Renormalizing the percolated lattice yields a regular resource, so loss tolerance is a percolation problem.
sources: Kieling, Rudolph & Eisert (2007). "Percolation, Renormalization, and Quantum Computing with Nondeterministic Gates". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 99, 130501. [arXiv:quant-ph/0611140](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0611140)

name: SYK model began as a quantum spin glass
summary: The Sachdev–Ye random all-to-all Heisenberg magnet, introduced to study a quantum spin-glass/spin-liquid transition, became (as SYK) the canonical maximally chaotic quantum system. Random couplings, large-N and replica tools come straight from spin-glass theory.
sources: Sachdev & Ye (1993). "Gapless spin-fluid ground state in a random quantum Heisenberg magnet". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 70, 3339. [arXiv:cond-mat/9212030](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9212030)

name: Spin-glass ground states and quantum annealing
summary: NP-hard optimization problems map onto spin-glass (Ising) ground-state searches. Quantum annealing replaces thermal fluctuations with a transverse field, and RSB landscapes and small gaps at first-order transitions limit its speedup.
sources: Kadowaki & Nishimori (1998). "Quantum annealing in the transverse Ising model". *Phys. Rev. E* 58, 5355. [arXiv:cond-mat/9804280](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9804280)
Lucas (2014). "Ising formulations of many NP problems". *Front. Phys.* 2, 5. [arXiv:1302.5843](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.5843)

name: Toric-code threshold as a random-bond Ising transition
summary: Optimal decoding of the surface code under independent bit-flip noise maps onto the 2D random-bond Ising model on the Nishimori line. The error threshold p_c≈10.9% is that model's ordering transition, and spin-glass replica tools now analyze qLDPC codes.
sources: Dennis et al. (2002). "Topological quantum memory". *J. Math. Phys.* 43, 4452. [arXiv:quant-ph/0110143](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0110143)

name: Quantum gases as statistical-mechanics laboratories
summary: Dilute ultracold Bose and Fermi gases realize textbook equilibrium statistical mechanics (ideal and weakly interacting BE/FD gases, BEC, degenerate Fermi pressure) with tunable interactions and traps.
sources: Dalfovo et al. (1998). "Theory of Bose-Einstein condensation in trapped gases". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 71, 463. [arXiv:cond-mat/9806038](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9806038)

name: Why isolated quantum systems look thermal
summary: ETH supplies the quantum-mechanical foundation that equilibrium statistical mechanics assumes. Individual energy eigenstates already give microcanonical expectation values for few-body observables, so ergodicity is not needed.
sources: D'Alessio et al. (2016). "From quantum chaos and eigenstate thermalization to statistical mechanics and thermodynamics". *Adv. Phys.* 65, 239. [arXiv:1509.06411](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.06411)

name: Negative absolute temperature in optical lattices
summary: A Bose–Hubbard gas with an upper-bounded energy spectrum (via band truncation and attractive U) was prepared at negative temperature, the textbook two-level-system case realized for motional degrees of freedom. It also revived the Gibbs-vs-Boltzmann entropy debate.
sources: Braun et al. (2013). "Negative Absolute Temperature for Motional Degrees of Freedom". *Science* 339, 52. [arXiv:1211.0545](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.0545)

name: Ensemble equivalence from eigenstate thermalization
summary: Under ETH the diagonal ensemble of a quench equals the microcanonical ensemble, which by ensemble equivalence equals the canonical one for local observables. Integrable systems need a generalized Gibbs ensemble instead.
sources: D'Alessio et al. (2016). "From quantum chaos and eigenstate thermalization to statistical mechanics and thermodynamics". *Adv. Phys.* 65, 239. [arXiv:1509.06411](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.06411)

name: Canonical typicality from entanglement
summary: For almost every pure state of a large system plus bath with fixed total energy, the reduced state of a small subsystem is close to canonical. Entanglement with the bath, not ensemble averaging over ignorance, explains the canonical ensemble.
sources: Popescu, Short & Winter (2006). "Entanglement and the foundations of statistical mechanics". *Nat. Phys.* 2, 754. [arXiv:quant-ph/0511225](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0511225)

name: Wick rotation: Z as an imaginary-time path integral
summary: Tr e^{-βH} is a Feynman path integral over paths periodic in imaginary time with period βħ. Quantum statistical mechanics in d dimensions is therefore classical statistical mechanics of polymers or fields in d+1 dimensions, which is the basis of path-integral Monte Carlo for helium.
sources: Feynman (1953). "Atomic Theory of the λ Transition in Helium". *Phys. Rev.* 91, 1291. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.91.1291](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.91.1291)

name: Landauer, demons and quantum resource theories
summary: Landauer erasure, Szilard engines and Maxwell demons generalize to qubits, where entanglement and coherence change the bookkeeping (negative conditional entropy can allow work extraction during erasure). Resource theories of athermality replace the free energy with a family of Rényi free energies for single-shot processes.
sources: Parrondo, Horowitz & Sagawa (2015). "Thermodynamics of information". *Nat. Phys.* 11, 131. [doi:10.1038/nphys3230](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys3230)

name: Thermal entropy as eigenstate entanglement entropy
summary: In a thermalizing pure state, a subsystem's entanglement entropy equals the thermodynamic entropy at the effective temperature (volume law). This was measured in a quantum gas microscope, where entanglement entropy became thermal entropy.
sources: Kaufman et al. (2016). "Quantum thermalization through entanglement in an isolated many-body system". *Science* 353, 794. [arXiv:1603.04409](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04409)

name: Information is physical: qubits and thermodynamics
summary: Quantum information inherits Shannon theory and Landauer's principle. Reversible unitary gates dissipate nothing in principle, but resetting ancillas and measurement records costs at least k_BT ln2 per bit.
sources: Landauer (1961). "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process". *IBM J. Res. Dev.* 5, 183. [doi:10.1147/rd.53.0183](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183)

name: Shannon, von Neumann and entanglement entropy
summary: The von Neumann entropy of a reduced density matrix is the quantum Shannon entropy and measures entanglement for pure bipartite states. It reduces to Gibbs entropy for thermal states.
